translations.text: Thus Alfred, king of the West Saxons, told us an old story. He displayed his skill, the craft of the poet.

He had a great desire to tell songs to these people, mirth to men, sayings of many kinds, so that boredom would not drive away the self-satisfied man, who cares little for such things because of his pride.
I must speak further, take up the song, and tell men counsel that is known among the people. Let whoever will, listen!

It was long ago that the Goths came from the east, out of Scythia, bearing shields. In a great host they overran many a nation's land, and in the south they established two victorious peoples. The kingdom of the Goths grew year by year.
They had two kings of their own kin, Radagaisus and Alaric. They prospered in power.
Then many a Goth was drawn over the Alps, full of boasting and eager for battle, for war between peoples. The banner swirled, bright on its staff.

The warriors, the shield-fighters, meant to overrun all Italy. And they did it, all the way from the Alps to the famous shore where Sicily, a great island in the sea-streams, makes its homeland renowned.

Then the kingdom of the Romans was conquered, the finest of cities was sacked, and Rome was laid open to the warriors. Radagaisus and Alaric went into the stronghold. The emperor fled with the princes away to the Greeks.

Then the wretched survivors could not hold out against the Goths in battle. The guardians of the homeland gave up, against their will, the treasures of their forefathers, and swore holy oaths. Either way there was woe.
Yet the young men's hearts were with the Greeks, if they had dared to follow a leader of the people.
Things stood that way for a time. The people had been conquered for many winters, until fate decreed that thegns and nobles should obey Theodoric.
The army's leader was bound to Christ; the king himself received the rite of baptism. All the children of the Romans rejoiced and quickly sought peace with him.
He firmly promised them that they could keep each of their ancient rights with honour in the wealthy city, for as long as God wished him to hold power over the Goths. He broke that whole promise.
To that prince the heresy of Arius was dearer than the law of the Lord.
He ordered John, the good pope, to be beheaded. That was no noble deed.
Besides that, the Goth committed countless other crimes against every good man.
Then in the city of Rome there was a certain powerful man who had been raised up as a leader. He was dear to his lord while the Greeks held the royal throne.
He was a righteous man. For a long time afterward there was no better giver of treasure among the Romans.
He was wise in the ways of the world, eager for honours, a man learned in books. The hero who won that fame was called Boethius.

At all times he kept in mind the evil and insult that foreign kings had shown him. He was loyal to the Greeks. He remembered the honours and ancient rights, the love and favours, that his ancestors had long enjoyed among them.
Then he began to think cunningly and earnestly about how he might bring the Greeks back there, so that the emperor might once again hold power over them.

He secretly sent letters to the old lords. By the Lord and by their old loyalty he begged them to come back to them in the city, to let the Greek counsellors govern the Romans, and to let the people have their rights.
When Theodoric the Amaling learned of that plan, he seized the thegn and ordered his companions to hold the warrior fast.
His mind was fierce, and he feared the nobleman. He ordered him to be locked inside a prison cell.
Then Boethius's mind was greatly troubled. For a long time before, he had enjoyed splendour under the heavens, so he could bear that time all the worse when it came on him so harshly.
Then the nobleman was in despair. He expected no mercy and could think of no comfort in that prison. Instead he fell face down to the floor, stretched out, and spoke many words, deeply despondent:
He did not expect ever to come out of those fetters. He called to the Lord in a mournful voice and sang this song:
"Lo, once I gladly sang many songs in happy times. Now, sighing, worn out with weeping, a sad exile, I must sing words of sorrow.
This sighing, this sobbing, has hindered me, so that I cannot compose songs as beautifully, though I once composed many true sayings when I was happy.
Now I often get familiar words wrong, though in the past I sometimes found unfamiliar ones."

"These worldly fortunes have foolishly led me, blind in almost everything, into this dark hole. They robbed me of counsel and comfort through their faithlessness, though I should always have been able to trust them most. They have bitterly turned their backs on me and taken their joy away from me."
when, struggling, it abandons its own light, and in woe forgets the eternal joy, and pushes into the darkness of this world, afflicted with sorrows.
"Lo, on earth all creatures obey your command, and in the heavens they do the same with heart and strength, except for man alone, who very often acts against your will."
"Throughout earthly kingdoms evil men sit on high seats and trample the holy under their feet. Men do not know why fate should turn so wrongly."

Just as a spring often wells up, cool and clear, from a grey cliff and flows smoothly and straight, running toward its home, until a great stone from the mountain falls into it and lies in its middle, rolled down from the crag.
so now the darkness of your heart will resist my bright teaching and greatly trouble the thoughts of your mind.
and too uplifted because of carefree worldly prosperity, nor again too feebly despair of any good, when the most adverse of things in the world oppress you and you weigh most heavily upon yourself.
For the mind is always greatly bound with trouble if either of these evils may afflict it and torment it within.
For those two griefs draw together a confusing mist in front of the mind, so that the eternal sun cannot shine through within it because of the dark mists, until they are lessened.
Then Wisdom again unlocked his word-hoard, sang true sayings, and spoke as follows:
When the sun shines most clearly, brightest from heaven, all the other stars over the earth are quickly darkened, because their brightness is nothing to set against the light of the sun.
When the wind beneath the clouds blows gently from the south and west, the flowers of the field quickly grow, glad that they are able to.

But the strong storm, when it comes mightily from the north and east, quickly takes away the beauty of the rose; and the northern tempest also forcibly drives the broad sea, so that, violently stirred up, it beats upon the shores.
Alas, that on earth nothing of steadfast work ever endures in the world!

Then Wisdom began to follow his custom: he sang in words of song, a lay after his discourse, and sang yet some true sayings. He said that he had not heard that any man could set up a firm-roofed hall on a high mountain.
Nor need any man expect to achieve the work of ever mingling wisdom with pride.
Have you ever heard that any man could set a firm hall on hills of sand? Nor can any man build wisdom where worldly greed overspreads the hill.
Bare sand will swallow up rain; so now does the bottomless greed of the powerful for glory and possessions: it drinks the perishing wealth dry, and yet the thirst of the needy one is not cooled.
No man can have a house on a mountain last long, because the swift wind suddenly sweeps upon it.
Nor is sand, any more, a guardian of a house for any man against heavy rain; rather it will fall, the sand will sink away after the rain.

In the same way the minds of all men are greatly shaken and stirred from their place when the strong wind of worldly hardships beneath the clouds afflicts them, or when the fierce rain of some anxiety, a boundless care, disturbs them again.

But he who wishes to possess the eternal, true happiness must strongly flee the beauty of this world, and then build for himself the house of his mind where he can find the stone of humility, immeasurably firm, a ready foundation;

it need not slide apart, though the wind of worldly hardships or the immense rain of cares should shake it, because in that valley of humility the Lord himself dwells, firmly settled, where wisdom ever dwells in remembrance.
Therefore wise men of the world always lead a carefree life without change,
when he despises all earthly goods and also remains untroubled by those evils, and hopes for the eternal things that come afterwards;
then almighty God continually and always keeps him on every side, abiding in the happiness of his own mind through the grace of the Creator, though the wind of worldly hardships greatly afflict him,
and constant care hinder him, when the wind of worldly fortune blows grimly and wrathfully upon him, though anxiety about these worldly fortunes always cruelly torment him.
As soon as Wisdom had clearly set out these words, he began to sing true sayings, and spoke as follows:
Lo, the first age was good for every earth-dweller throughout the surface of the earth, when to each one the fruits of the earth seemed enough. It is not so now!
There were then no wealthy homes throughout the world, nor various foods and drinks, nor indeed did they care for the garments which nobles now regard as most precious.
For none of them existed yet. Seafarers had not seen them and had not heard of them anywhere around.

Lo, they were not greedy for sinful lusts, except so far as they might most moderately follow the nature which Christ shaped for them; and they ate once a day, always at evening, the fruits of the earth, of wood and herbs; they did not drink bright wine from a deep cup at all.
At that time there was no servant who knew how to mix food or drink, water with honey, nor how to sew their garments with silk,

Nor did they adorn fine cloth with cunning crafts, nor did they skilfully build jewelled halls; but they always, at all times, slept outdoors under the shade of trees, and drank the water of streams, of cold springs.
No merchant saw a foreign shore across the sea. People certainly had not heard of fleets of warships, and no man even spoke of battle.

"Do you think that the power of God Almighty could not easily strip that boastful wrongdoer of his kingdom and rob him of his power through his eternal might, or otherwise restrain him from his evil?"
To the wise-minded it can easily seem that this whole earth is immeasurably small compared with the other. To the unwise, however, it may seem vast and firm in its place, to a man without guidance,
O you proud ones, why do you always want to bow your necks, of your own will, under that heavy yoke?
Even if it should now be your fortune that the most distant earth-dwellers, south or north, praise you greatly in many languages, even if someone is noble by high birth and honoured with riches,
Where now also is the wise one, eager for honour, the steadfast shepherd of the people, who was a philosopher in every matter, bold and skilful, whose name was Cato?
That is also too little for such teachers, because those men deserved more in the world.
What then does any hero, any man, gain from that glory if eternal death may seize him after this world?

He is also the ruler of the world's creatures: of heaven and earth and the deep sea, and of all those that dwell in them, the invisible ones, and likewise of those we look on with our eyes, of all creatures.

So has the guardian of the heavenly kingdom constrained all creatures with his power that each of them strives against the other, and yet, while striving, they firmly support one another. Each embraces the other from outside, so that they do not slip apart.
Therefore they must always turn back again to the same course that the Father appointed at the beginning, and so become new once more.
So it now changes, the Lord's ancient work, so that the warring, opposed creation keeps a firm peace from then on.

But when the eternal and almighty one decides to let go the reins, those very bridles with which he bridled all his own work at the beginning (that is, the opposition of every creature, which we try to express by that bridle);
O God of victories, this mankind would be greatly blessed if their minds could be set steadfast and put in order by that strong power, just as the other creatures of the world are.
So to each earth-dweller true happiness always seems the better and the more delightful, the more torments and harsh afflictions he endures here.
You can also much more easily recognize true happiness more clearly in your mind, and afterwards come to know it,
The ruler of the heavens has so constrained all creatures, surrounded them from outside and bound them with his chain, that they cannot manage ever to slip away from him;
So now each thing in the wide creation strives toward that place, except some angels and mankind, of whom far too many among the world's dwellers fight against their nature.
No man need expect that she will keep her tameness well after that event. I think instead that she will pay no attention at all to her new tameness, but will remember the wild ways of her ancestors;
she begins in earnest to tear the chains, to roar, to growl, and first she bites the keeper of her own house, and quickly afterwards every man she can catch.
From then on they gladly live in the trees according to their wild ancestral nature, even if one of their teachers should skilfully offer them the same food with which he had tamed them before.
when they hear other birds warbling their notes, they stir up their own voices; all together they ring out a delightful song, and the wood answers them all.

So it is with all trees whose nature it is to grow highest in the wood: though you bend some bough down toward the earth, it goes upward again; as soon as you let the wood go free, it turns back to its nature.
So does the sun also: when it is going down after midday, the sea-candle hurries on its descent and ventures by night on an unknown way, north again and east;
it appears to people and brings the earth-dwellers a bright morning over the sea. It climbs ever upward over mankind until it comes again to where its highest place, its natural home, is.
Just as every creature throughout this wide world strives and hastens with all its might, so it always turns back again with all its might and returns to its own nature when it can.
There is now no creature on earth that does not long to come back to the homeland it came from. That homeland is freedom from care and eternal rest; that is, plainly, almighty God.
There is now no creature on earth that does not turn upon itself, as a wheel does. For it turns in such a way that it comes back to where it was before;
when it has first been turned outward, when it has been turned wholly outward, it must afterwards do again what it did before, and also be what it was before.
What is the rich, greedy man of the world the better for it in his mind, even if he owns much gold and gems and goods of every kind, possessions beyond counting,
and even if a thousand acres had to be ploughed for him every day, and even if this world and this race of men under the sun, south, west and east, were all made subject to his rule?
He may not take any more of those ornaments, those hoarded treasures, away from this world than he brought into it.

Though the wicked, unrighteous King Nero newly arrayed himself wonderfully in beautiful garments, adorned with gold and with gems of every kind, yet in his lifetime every wise man in the world thought him hateful, worthless and full of sin.
Yet the fiend raised up his favourites with honours.

Yet I cannot understand why they should ever be the happier in their minds for that. Even if the most foolish of kings chose them for a while, though they had no virtues, they were none the worthier for it in the eyes of any of the wise.
Though the fool makes him king, how can a man of good judgement explain that he is, or seems, any better for it?

Whoever wishes to have power must first strive to have power over himself inwardly, in his own mind, so that he is never wholly subject to his vices. Let him put out of his mind the many different cares that are useless to him, and let him for a while leave off lamenting his miseries.
Even if all this middle-earth, as the ocean currents surround it, were given to him to possess, as far as an island now lies westernmost out in the ocean,

where there is no night in summer, and no more in winter is the day divided into hours, which is called Thule; even if one man alone now ruled all that island, and also everything from there eastward as far as the Indians;

Though he may now own all that, why is his power any greater if he afterwards has no control over his own mind, and does not earnestly and carefully guard himself, in words and deeds, against the vices we are speaking of?

Lo, all the inhabitants of the earth, the dwellers on the land, had a like beginning. They all came into the world from just two people, a man and a woman, and they all still come into the world alike now, the proud and the lowly.
That is no wonder, because all wise men know that there is one God of all creatures, Lord of mankind, Father and Creator.
He gives the light of the sun from the heavens, and of the moon and these glorious stars.
The merciful Lord created men on earth and joined soul to body at the very beginning; he created people under the clouds, every man, equally noble.
Why then do you ever arrogantly exalt yourselves over other men without cause, since you find no one who is ignoble?
Why do you raise yourselves up because of your noble birth, since the true nobility I am telling you about lies in the mind of every man, and not at all in the flesh of the dwellers on earth?
But now every man who is wholly subject to his vices first abandons the origin of his life, and likewise his own noble birth, and also the Father who created him in the beginning.
For almighty God makes him ignoble, so that from then on he becomes forever ignoble in the world and does not come to glory.
Alas, how much wrong is done by the evil, wrathful desire for adultery, which troubles the mind of nearly every member of the human race completely.
Lo, the wild bee, wise though it is, must perish utterly if it stings anything in anger.
In the same way every soul must afterwards be lost if the body becomes defiled by unlawful intercourse, unless repentance first comes into the person's heart before he departs from here.
Alas, let anyone who will think about it: it is grievous folly, and dangerous to every man, which leads wretched men utterly astray, so that they are quickly led away from the right path.
Will you look in the woods for red gold on green trees?
Yet I know that no wise man looks for it there, because it does not grow there, nor do beautiful gems grow in vineyards.
It is a wonder, as we all know, that people must seek noble gems along the seashore and the riverbanks: white and red, and of every colour.
Because they never wish to search after them, to seek those blessings. Half-wise, they think that in this passing life they may find true blessings, that is, God himself.
O my Lord, you are almighty, great, magnificent, famed for glories, and wonderful to every wise man.
There is none mightier and none more glorious, nor any equal to you throughout all creation, nor did you ever yet have any need of all the works that you have made;
Great is the nature of your goodness, let whoever will reflect on it, for in every respect it is all one, you and your goodness.
It is your own, because nothing at all came to you from outside. I know well that your goodness, almighty Good, is wholly within yourself.
It is unlike our nature: everything good that we have on earth has come to us from outside, from God himself.
but the thanes, the king's warriors, are brought into harmony together, cold with heat and wet with dry, though they still strive against each other.
Therefore leaves and grass spread throughout Britain, blooming and growing for the benefit of men. The cold earth brings forth many wonderful fruits, because it is moistened with water.
If that were not so, it would be dried to dust and then scattered far and wide by the wind, just as ashes are now often blown all over the earth.
and by your skill you tempered cold and heat, so that the fire cannot burn the land and the sea-stream pale, though it is firmly joined with both, the Father's ancient work.
That is the proper power of the sea-stream, of water and earth, and also in the clouds, and likewise up above the sky.

Though it is mingled again with all the creatures of the world, yet it has no power to destroy any of them completely without the leave of him who granted us this life, that is, the eternal and almighty one.

Earth is heavier than the other creatures and more densely packed, because it has long stood lowest of all creatures, except the sky, which every day revolves around this spacious creation from outside,
None of them can exist without the others.
It is the greatest power of a man's soul and the best of its particular skills.

Lo, you, Ruler of victories, glorious King of peoples, created the soul so that it should turn upon itself and around itself, just as the whole swift-running heaven does, swiftly circling this middle-earth each day by the Lord's power.
Lo, you, eternal God, also mingle heavenly things here with earth, souls with body; after that the earthly and the eternal dwell together, soul in flesh.

Enlighten now the eyes of our mind with your light, Ruler of life, for you are the brightness of true light, gracious Father, and you yourself, Father almighty, are the firm resting-place of all the righteous.
That is the one haven that will always be calm after the waves of our toils, after every storm.
But I know for certain that golden treasure, a silver jewel, any cunning gem, or the wealth of the world will never enlighten the eyes of the mind,
nor improve their sharpness at all for seeing true happiness. Instead, they blind the mind's eyes in every man's breast rather than make them brighter.
For everything that pleases in this present life is fleeting: earthly things that are always passing away.
But wondrous is that beauty and brightness that brightens the beauty of every creature and then rules over them all.
The Ruler does not want our souls to perish. He himself, the Ruler of life, will light them with his radiance.
If, then, any man can ever see with the clear eyes of his mind the pure brightness of heaven's light,
he will say that, compared with that great light of God Almighty, the brightness of the sun is darkness to every man. That light is eternal, without end, for every spirit, for blessed souls.

Whoever wants to search inwardly, rightly and with good judgement, so deeply that no man can scatter it and no earthly thing can spoil it, must first look within himself for what he had for some time been seeking around him.
Let him then seek it within his mind, and let him give up, as often as he can, every care that is useless to him, and let him gather, as fully as he can,
all his inner thought on that one thing. Let him tell his mind that it can find within itself everything it now so often and so constantly seeks outside itself: every good.
He will then see that all he had long kept in his inner chamber was evil and useless, just as clearly as he can look at the sun with his own eyes,
and he will also see that his inner thought is lighter and brighter than the sun's beam in summer, when the gem of the sky, the bright heavenly star, shines most clearly.
For the vices and heaviness of the body and its bad habits can never wholly draw righteousness out of the mind of any man;
Yet the sins, the heaviness and the vices of the body now often trouble every man's mind, most of all through evil forgetfulness.
With a mist of error it covers the sorrowing heart, the mind of every man, so that the mind cannot gleam and shine as brightly as it would if it had the power to.
yet some grain of the seed of truth is always kept in the soul, as long as the spirit dwells joined together with the body.
Still, the grain of that seed is always awakened by questioning, and afterwards also by good teaching, if it is to grow.
How can any man, a person with reason, find an answer about anything, even if someone questions him properly, if he has in his mind nothing, great or small, of righteousness or understanding?
Yet there is no man so entirely bereft of understanding that he cannot find any answer in his mind if he is asked.
So the old philosopher, our Plato, once told us a true saying. He said that anyone who has forgotten righteousness should quickly turn back into the memory of his mind.

There, in his secret chamber, in his spirit, he can then find righteousness firmly hidden. It is hidden above all by the daily turmoil of his mind, by the heaviness of his body, and by the cares that constantly stir in a man's breast and mind.
Lo, that man on earth is blessed in every way who can see the clearest, heaven-bright stream, the noble spring of every good, and can cast off from himself the dark mist, the darkness of the mind.
Yet, with God's help, we must still improve your inner thought with old and made-up fables, so that you may better find the right path up to the heavens, into the eternal home of our souls.
I have feathers swifter than a bird's, and with them I can fly far from the earth, over the high roof of this heaven. If I could now give feathers to the mind,
[?] your heart, with my feathers, until you could wholly despise this middle-earth and every earthly thing.
you could soar fittingly on feathers above the skies, wind your way far up over the clouds, and then look down from above over everything.
You could also pass over the fire that has long moved for many years between the air and the heavens, as the Father appointed for it in the beginning.

If you travel rightly, so that you leave the highest heaven behind you, then afterwards you may have your share of the true light, from where the one King reigns far and wide, up above the heavens and likewise below, over all creatures, and rules the world.
That is the wise King; that is he who rules over all the other kings of the earth throughout the nations of men, who with his bridle has bound the whole circuit of earth and heaven.
I will never wish to go out from here; rather I will always stand here firmly and at ease, by the Father's will."
that they are always very poor and powerless in everything, even those very ones whom this wretched people now for a while fears most.
and the lord who rules the army has no regard for friend or foe, for life or possessions, but rushes savagely upon everyone, most like a mad dog;
I can explain that from excess in everything, in food and clothing, in wine-drinking and in sweetmeats, there grows most strongly the great madness of lust;
it greatly troubles the inner thought of every man's mind, and from it come most of the evils of arrogance and useless quarrels.
When they become enraged, the mind within their breast is beaten in the heart by the strong surge of hot temper, and soon afterwards it is also bound by sadness and held hard captive.
Then some hope begins to lie to him greatly about vengeance for that strife; his anger desires one thing and another; his recklessness promises him all of it and has no regard for what is right.
I told you earlier in this same book that every single one of the wide creatures always desired some good, according to its own ancient nature.
What is worse still is that he will not strive against that power at any time;
When Ulysses, king of the Thracians, had leave to depart from there, he left behind him ninety-nine beaked ships.

Then came cold weather, a fierce tumult of storms. The dark wave crashed against another and drove the band of warriors far out onto the Mediterranean, up onto the island where Apollo's daughter had lived for a great number of days.
She, a king's daughter, followed error more than anyone among many peoples. Among the hosts she was called Circe.

She loved the lord of the seafarers with boundless tenderness, and he likewise, with all his strength, loved her in his heart just as greatly. So he felt no desire in his mind for his homeland, beyond the young maiden.

Instead he lived with the woman after that, until none of his thanes could stay there with him any longer. Because of those miseries they longed for their homeland and meant to abandon their dear lord.
Lo, the foolish men who long believed in these sorceries, these false tales, still knew that no one can change the mind and understanding by sorcery.
From such things as these you can clearly see that the skills and powers of the body come from the mind, for every man, each single one.

None among the people need expect the outcome that the weary flesh could ever wholly turn the mind of any man to itself. Rather, the vices of each mind and the inner thought of each man lead the body wherever it wishes.
Why must you always trouble your minds with unjust hatreds, as the waves of the sea-flood stir the ice-cold sea and toss it before the wind? Why do you blame your fate, which has no power?
Why can you not wait for the death, bitter by nature, that the Lord has ordained for you, now that it hastens toward you every day?
Can you not see that it is always on the track of every offspring of the earth, beasts and birds alike?
But it is wrong for any man to hate another in his heart with malicious thoughts, as a bird or a beast does. It would be most right for each man to give the other a just reward,

those that move about the end of the axle, or those that travel much more widely, rushing mightily around its middle? One of these is called Saturn, which takes about thirty years by count to go around the world.

Unsteady people always think that something in the ancient creation they seldom see never existed before. Even more, worldly men think it came about by chance as a new happening if it never appeared to any of them before. That is a wretched thing.

Therefore almighty God does not leave them alone on one half of this heaven, lest they destroy other noble creatures. Instead, the eternal God moderates all the wide creation and gently brings it into harmony.
Sometimes the dry drives out the wet. Sometimes, by the Creator's skill, he mixes cold with heat. Sometimes the all-bright flame, light in the air, turns back again to the sky above.
yet all the creatures of heaven and earth share one love in common: that they serve such a Lord of peoples and rejoice that their Father rules.
That is no wonder, because no creature could ever survive otherwise if it did not serve its origin, the glorious Lord, with all its might.
Homer lived in the east among the Greeks and was the most skilled of poets in that nation. He was the friend and teacher of Virgil, the best of masters to that famous poet.
Lo, that Homer often and repeatedly praised the beauty of the sun greatly, and often and repeatedly told people of its noble powers in songs and stories.
Yet even though it is clear and bright, it cannot shine anywhere near all created things. And even the created things it can shine on, it cannot light up all together, both inside and out.
It is not fitting that any man's mind should be bent downward while his face is turned upward!
